results.summary: Checked the whole section field by field against the current official text of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18 on malegislature.gov, 105 CMR 721.055 and 247 CMR 9.04 fetched and inflated from the mass.gov PDFs, and 21 CFR 1306.22 on eCFR, all on 2026-09-12. The three pathways are attached to the right subsections and the right windows: s. 18(c) reaches schedules III to VI and is 'valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions, issued within the preceding thirty days'; s. 18(d) (nonnarcotic Schedule II) and s. 18(d1/2) (narcotic Schedule II, except as provided in s. 18A, from Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth) each reach only 'the filling of prescriptions within the commonwealth, issued within the preceding 5 days'. The section's insistence that the window is measured to the fill rather than to presentation follows the word 'preceding' in each paragraph. The issuing conditions are reproduced with the distinction the statute actually draws -- 'the state wherein he resides' in (c) against 'another state where he resides or practices' in (d) and (d1/2) -- and all three do require federal registration to write prescriptions. The verification analysis is correct and is the section's sharpest teaching point: s. 18(c) imposes the authenticity and validity determination on every prescription it reaches but conditions telephone verification on the substance being 'in schedules III to V, inclusive', while s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) each state the verification duty for their own Schedule II route, so Schedule VI is indeed the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without it; the liability shield for refusing is correctly conditioned on documented good faith efforts. The two five-day rules are kept apart correctly: the s. 18(d)/(d1/2) filling window against the s. 18(d3/4) limit on the initial partial dispensing of a prescription 'filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2)', with the 30-day remainder clock and the same-pharmacy restriction attached to the latter, and 105 CMR 721.055(A) correctly reported as stating that limit as presentation 'not later than five calendar days after the Prescription issue date' where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth. 247 CMR 9.04(10) is quoted accurately. The Department copy is correctly keyed to 30 days after the filling, anonymised, and not a public record. The later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) are the part most likely to be got wrong and are got right: each of the six conditions is reproduced, the prescriber condition is measured against the state of delivery, the pharmacist licensure and the 'authentic, valid, legitimate and legal' determination against the originating state, and the full-compliance and reporting conditions against the delivery state -- which is what 'that state' in condition (4) refers back to. The long-term care paragraph is correctly reported as stating no separate prescriber condition and as requiring courier delivery directly to the facility. Absolute words are all supported: 'every one of the three subsections', 'all three require federal registration', 'only the same pharmacy', 'the single pathway' and 'nothing in the section authorizes a mail order pharmacy' each track statutory text. All four mapped practice questions (MA-Q-0027, MA-Q-0034, MA-Q-0124, MA-Q-0424) are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it. No finding.

results.summary: Checked the whole section field by field against 21 CFR 1308.01, 1308.11 through 1308.15, 1300.01(a) and 21 U.S.C. 802(18), and against M.G.L. c. 94C ss. 1, 2, 2A, 23(f) and 24A and 105 CMR 700.001, 700.002 and 700.012 (current 2024 edition of the 105 CMR 700.000 PDF, fetched and inflated in the browser), all on 2026-09-12. The federal architecture is stated accurately: 21 CFR 1308.01 places the section 202 schedules in 1308.11 through 1308.15, each of those sections opens with the quoted 'shall consist of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name...' sentence, and the section's hedge that 'most of them' add the code-number sentence is right (1308.15 does not). The reliance on defined terms is correct: 1300.01(a) sends an undefined term to 21 U.S.C. 802, and 802(18) defines opiate/opioid by addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability similar to morphine or capability of conversion, which is what the 1308.12(b)(1) class listing carries. Every substance the section names as excluded from that listing, samidorphan included, is in fact inside its exclusion clause together with 'their respective salts', and the section is careful to say only that the exclusion decides paragraph (b)(1) and not the other paragraphs. The quantity and formulation examples are exact: codeine at 1308.12(b)(1)(i); 1308.13(e)(1)(ii) at not more than 1.8 g per 100 mL or 90 mg per dosage unit with active nonnarcotic ingredients in recognized therapeutic amounts; 1308.15(c)(1) at not more than 200 mg per 100 mL or per 100 g, read with the (c) chapeau's 'sufficient proportion to confer ... valuable medicinal qualities other than those possessed by narcotic drugs alone'; and difenoxin at 1308.14(b)(1) and 1308.15(c)(6). The overlap in the second worked example is resolved through the 1308.13(e) preface, which is the paragraph that actually carries it. The Massachusetts half is the sovereignty point and is attributed correctly: 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) do currently define Schedules I through V as the drugs listed in the matching federal sections and 700.002(F) defines Schedule VI as 'all prescription drugs, which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner', so a Schedule VI drug is one no federal schedule lists; and because s. 1 defines a controlled substance as one in any schedule or class the chapter refers to and s. 2(a) makes the sixth schedule one of them, a Schedule VI drug is a Massachusetts controlled substance, which is why s. 23(f)'s refill condition -- written for controlled substances without a Schedule VI carve-out -- reaches it. Monitoring is attributed to the right instrument: s. 24A(a)(1) reaches schedule II to V controlled substances and additional drugs, 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a Schedule VI controlled substance so determined, 700.012(A)(1) states the pharmacy duty and (A)(2) excludes dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient, and 700.012(C)(8) supplies the determination and the notice to dispensers, with the four factors as described. The 'no federal counterpart' claim for Schedule VI is supported, as is s. 2A's 14-day notice period, one-year maximum and s. 2A(f) referral to the United States Attorney General, and 21 CFR 1308.11(h) is where an emergency-scheduled substance is listed, inside Schedule I. No practice questions are mapped to this section, so nothing can be contradicted. No finding.
